world.title: African STEM education in the age of global S&T asymmetry
world.description: Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education has become central to Africa’s development aspirations and technological transformation. However, persistent gaps in scientific capability, technological agency, and innovation outcomes continue to widen. This article examines how global science and technology (S&T) asymmetry shapes African STEM education systems: structurally, institutionally, and epistemically. Using a conceptual analytical approach, the study analyzes how inherited institutional cultures and structures, economic constraints, epistemic hierarchies, and emerging digital dependencies converge to influence STEM education systems across the continent. The analysis is organized around four interconnected domains: systemic foundations, curriculum packages, human capital, and innovation ecosystems. Across these domains, the findings show that African STEM education systems are deeply embedded in externally shaped policy frameworks, donor-driven priorities, and global benchmarking regimes. At the policy level, reliance on imported models and weak coordination undermines long-term system building. At the practice level, fragile institutional capacity, inadequate funding and infrastructure, talent loss, and fragmented innovation systems constrain meaningful implementation. These conditions weaken the capacity of STEM education to inspire learners, support teachers, foster technological agency, and connect scientific learning to local problem-solving and development pathways. Drawing on illustrative country cases and development experiences from non-African contexts, the article argues that Africa’s STEM education challenges are primarily structural and institutional. The paper concludes by outlining general pathways for strengthening African STEM education via reclaiming policy autonomy, ecosystem-based approaches, strategic public investment, and alignment with national and continental development priorities.

business.title: Olaparib plus tremelimumab in women with recurrent ovarian cancer and a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation: a phase I/II study
business.description: Response rates to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in ovarian cancer are low. In preclinical studies, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibition (PARPi) synergized with CTLA4 ICB to achieve long-term survival in Brca1-deficient ovarian cancer models. Here we evaluated the safety and efficacy of combined treatment with the PARPi olaparib and the CTLA4 ICB tremelimumab for recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer in a multi-site single-arm phase I/II study enrolling 50 women with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations (NCT02571725). In phase I, no new toxicities were identified (n = 3). In the combined phase I and II safety cohort (n = 49), 57% of subjects experienced grade 3 or 4 non-hematologic toxicity, with tremelimumab discontinuation in 34.7%. The primary phase II endpoint, overall response rate was 32.7% (95% CI 19.5-45.8%), and disease control rate was 47.7% (95% CI 33.0-62.5%). Secondary outcomes were progression-free survival (PFS, 3.0 months, 95% CI 2.7-5.9), and overall survival (24.3 months, CI 14.9-30.4). In exploratory post-hoc biomarker analyses, low VSTM5 or IFIT1B expression was associated with treatment benefit and improved PFS (p < 0.001). Although the trial did not meet its prespecified efficacy endpoint, PFS > 12 months in 6 subjects among this heavily pre-treated cohort highlight the need for biomarkers to select regimens for patients with recurrent ovarian cancer. Response rate to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in ovarian cancer remains low and combinatorial strategies are needed. Here the authors report the results of a phase I/II study of the PARP inhibitor olaparib and the anti-CTLA4 antibody tremelimumab in women with recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer and a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation.

science.title: Spatial variation shapes gut microbiome composition and functional potential in an Afrotropical fish
science.description: Host-associated microbiomes are shaped by environmental heterogeneity across spatial gradients. However, the extent to which site-level variation structures gut microbial communities in Afrotropical fishes remains poorly resolved. In this study, we employed high-throughput 16S rRNA gene sequencing to characterize the gut microbiome of the African forktail catfish (Chrysichthys nigrodigitatus) encompassing two contrasting habitat types, with the aim of assessing spatial patterns in microbial composition and predicted functional potential. Across all sites, gut microbial communities were dominated by Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, Bacteroidota, and Fusobacteriota, with a conserved core microbiome shared among populations. Alpha diversity metrics (Observed richness, Shannon, Simpson, and Chao1 indices) did not differ significantly among sites, indicating comparable levels of microbial richness and evenness. In contrast, beta diversity analysis based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarity revealed pronounced site-specific structuring and clear differentiation between habitat types. Differential abundance and indicator taxa analyses identified distinct bacterial assemblages associated with specific habitats, reflecting localized environmental influences. Functional predictions indicated enrichment of pathways related to xenobiotic degradation, oxidative stress response, and aromatic compound metabolism in lagoon habitat. The concordance between taxonomic composition and predicted functional profiles underscores the role of site variation in shaping gut microbiome structure. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that spatial variation is a key determinant of gut microbiome composition and predicted functional capacity in this widely distributed Afrotropical fish species, providing new insights into host-microbiome-environment interactions in tropical aquatic systems.
